hints: Look at the names ethanal, propanal and propanone. The endings in al and one tell you they belong to the same family, think about what $C=O$ group they all share.
walkthrough:
Spot the family from the names**
You have ethanal, propanal and propanone. The al ending means aldehyde and the one ending means ketone. At AS level both of these families are built around the same functional group, so you only need one name.

Name the shared group**
Both aldehydes ($RCHO$) and ketones ($RCOR$) contain a carbon doubly bonded to oxygen. That is the carbonyl group, $C=O$. It is the reactive centre in all three compounds.

hints: Recall the general test that gives a coloured crystalline precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones, but not with other functional groups.
Remember the characteristic colour of the hydrazone precipitate formed in that test, it is a bright orange, yellow or red solid.
walkthrough:
Choose a test for all carbonyls**
You need one reagent that reacts with both aldehydes and ketones in the same way. That is 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, often shortened to 2,4-DNPH. It undergoes a condensation reaction with the $C=O$ group to form a 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone.

State the positive observation**
When a carbonyl compound is present, an orange, yellow or red precipitate appears. Since F, G and H all contain a carbonyl group, all three would give this same precipitate, confirming they share the functional group.

Final answer: reagent: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH)
observation: orange / yellow / red precipitate

hints: Use Tollens reagent first to split the three compounds. Think about which type, aldehyde or ketone, gives a silver mirror and which shows no change.
Use alkaline $I_{2}(aq)$ next to split them further. Recall that only molecules containing the $CH_{3}CO$ group give a pale yellow precipitate in this test.
walkthrough:
Sort with Tollens reagent**
Tollens reagent contains the complex ion $[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}$. It is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes to carboxylic acids but cannot oxidise ketones. A positive result is a silver mirror. From Table 6.1, G and H give a silver mirror, so they are the two aldehydes, ethanal and propanal. F shows no change, so F must be the ketone, propanone.

Sort with alkaline iodine**
Alkaline $I_{2}(aq)$ is the iodoform test. A pale yellow precipitate of $CHI_{3}$ forms only if the molecule contains a $CH_{3}CO$ group. Both F (propanone, $CH_{3}COCH_{3}$) and G give the precipitate, so G must be the aldehyde that also has $CH_{3}CO$, which is ethanal, $CH_{3}CHO$. H gives no precipitate, so H must be propanal, $CH_{3}CH_{2}CHO$, which has no $CH_{3}CO$ group.

Final answer: F = propanone, $CH_{3}COCH_{3}$
G = ethanal, $CH_{3}CHO$
H = propanal, $CH_{3}CH_{2}CHO$

hints: Recall the name and formula of the pale yellow solid formed in a positive iodoform test with alkaline iodine.
walkthrough:
Name the yellow solid**
Whenever alkaline $I_{2}(aq)$ gives a pale yellow precipitate with a $CH_{3}CO$ compound, that solid is always the same product. It is tri-iodomethane, $CHI_{3}$, commonly called iodoform.

hints: Think beyond carbonyls. Which alcohol structure can be oxidised in situ by iodine to give a $CH_{3}CO$ group and therefore also give $CHI_{3}$?
walkthrough:
Link a non-carbonyl to the same precipitate**
You are told J does not have a carbonyl group but still gives $CHI_{3}$ with alkaline $I_{2}$. At AS level there is one other family that does this, alcohols containing the $CH_{3}CH(OH)$ unit. Under the test conditions iodine oxidises $CH_{3}CH(OH)R$ to $CH_{3}COR$, which then undergoes the normal iodoform reaction. So J must be an alcohol of the form $CH_{3}CH(OH)R$, for example ethanol where R is H, or propan-2-ol where R is $CH_{3}$.
Final answer: Compound J contains the group $CH_{3}CH(OH)$, e.g. $CH_{3}CH(OH)R$ where R is H or an alkyl group, such as ethanol $CH_{3}CH_{2}OH$ or propan-2-ol $CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3}$
